tagline.text: A museum of about 400 paintings by nine members of an Angono artist family

location.label: Location
location.text: 312 A. Ibañez Street, San Vicente, Angono, Rizal

best_season.label: Best time to visit
best_season.text: November–May dry season (late November, around the Higantes Festival, is recommended)

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱300–800 (per person, covering admission, café and tricycle)

children.text: The Blanco Family Museum displays about 400 works by the Angono-born painter José "Pitok" Blanco, his wife and their seven children. You can see the signature mural "Angono Fisherman's Festival," the studio and the garden café in a little over an hour.

The Blanco Family Museum is a private art museum in the town of Angono, Rizal. Angono, known in the Philippines as the "Arts Capital," produced the National Artists Carlos "Botong" Francisco and Lucio San Pedro, and the Blanco family carries that tradition forward as a family of painters. The museum opened in 1980 and displays about 400 works painted by family members over several decades.

The central figure is Pitok Blanco, a painter born in Angono. He entered the University of Santo Tomas fine arts program in 1951, graduated at the top of his class in 1955, worked at an advertising firm, and became a full-time painter in 1971. His wife, Loreto "Loring" Perez, began painting under her husband at the age of 48, and their children Glenn, Noel, Michael, Joy, Jan, Gay and Peter Paul all took up the brush. The family exhibition held at the National Museum in Manila in 1978 is described as the first in Philippine art history in which a father showed together with all his children. Pitok died on August 14, 2008, at the age of 76. His family is said to descend from Pedro Piñon, a 19th-century maker of religious paintings and sculpture. The couple taught their children like a small academy but did not force them into art, encouraging them to study fields that could also provide a steady income. In 1990 the family held an exhibition in Sentosa, Singapore, in which all nine members showed work, and in 2000 the couple received the Ulirang Ama and Ulirang Ina awards (model father and mother).

The exhibit is organized in an unusual way. The ground-floor halls devote one section to each of the nine family members. The sequence starts with the youngest, Peter Paul, and his childhood doodles, passes through the siblings, Glenn and his mother Loring, and ends in front of the murals of the father, Pitok. The upper floor is the atelier where the works were actually painted. Next to the exhibit halls are the Blanco Art Gallery, which sells works by other local artists, plus a garden and a café. The current curator is Michael Blanco, the third child. The family's style is mostly realist, but each member has different subjects, and Pitok became known as a muralist who painted prehistory, colonial history, Filipino festivals and folk traditions, and contemporary life.

This guide is for travelers who want to see Angono on a day trip from Manila. The museum alone takes one to two hours, so it pairs well with a walk through the Angono art town, lunch and nearby sights as a half-day plan. Fees and opening hours vary a little between sources, so it is safest to check with the museum or its Facebook page before you go.

This is Pitok Blanco's signature work, a large mural of Angono's town fiesta. It has more than 100 figures, and he spent two years going from house to house sketching the faces of real neighbors. The painter and his family appear in the picture too, so finding them becomes part of the fun.

This darker work depicts the tragedy of Angono during the Japanese occupation in World War II, and it hangs opposite the Fisherman's Festival mural. Comparing a bright festival with the scars of war in a single room is a memorable moment for visitors.

blocks.title: One section for each of the nine family members

children.text: The exhibit gives each family member a section. The museum leaflet lists the subjects as mother and child for Gay, feathered animals for Jan, cultural environment for Joy, lively figure groups for Michael, water for Noel, lush vegetation for Glenn and human warmth for Loring. Even within one family, the styles and subjects differ, which makes comparing them enjoyable. Following the display order, you can see naturally how one family influenced each other across generations.

The youngest, Peter Paul, is said to have started drawing at 11 months old, and his childhood doodles hang at the very start of the exhibit. This corner best conveys the atmosphere of a family in which art was part of daily life.

The studio where the works were actually painted is preserved on the second floor. With easels, paints and unfinished pictures, it feels livelier than the exhibit halls. Ask the staff on the day whether it is open.

This separate gallery attached to the family halls displays and sells works by Angono and nearby artists. If something catches your eye, you can ask directly about the price, packing and how to take it with you. Some travelers buy a small painting as a souvenir.

Outside the halls, the garden has chairs and leads to the café. It is a good place to rest after your visit, and the courtyard is used for workshops and events. On hot days the shaded seats fill up first.

blocks.title: Combine with a walk through the Angono art town

children.text: The museum sits in the middle of Angono, so it combines easily with town sights such as the Francisco house, galleries and street murals. You can read more about the town in the
Angono Art Town
guide.

items.subtitle: The museum and a walk through Angono

children.text: Take a jeepney or UV Express to Angono from a terminal along EDSA in Manila.
Get off in front of the Angono municipal hall and take a tricycle to the museum.
View the ground-floor halls in order and spend some time in front of the Fisherman's Festival mural.
Take a short break at the garden café and look around the gallery.
Have lunch at a restaurant in town, then walk the streets to see murals and galleries.
Opening hours and closing days differ between sources, so avoid Mondays and public holidays and check by phone or Facebook before you leave.
Leave Manila and head to Angono.
Visit the Blanco Family Museum.
Have lunch in Angono town.
Go on to Tanay by car or taxi and see the old town and church.
Head back toward Manila before sunset.
Manila East Road is congested at rush hour, so it is better to leave before 4:30 PM.
Take a jeepney or UV Express to Angono from the terminals near SM Megamall, Robinsons Galleria, Starmall EDSA-Shaw or Greenfield District in Mandaluyong.
From Pasig, board at the terminals near Marcos Highway, such as Sta. Lucia East Grandmall or Robinsons Metro East.
Get off in front of the Angono municipal hall and take a tricycle to the museum.
Travel time varies from about an hour and a half to three hours depending on traffic. Check current fares locally.
The address is 312 A. Ibañez Street, Angono. You can search for the museum by name on Waze.
From central Manila it usually takes one to two hours, and longer on weekends.
If you use a chartered taxi or Grab, finding a ride back can be difficult, so you can agree on a driver and waiting time in advance.
A tricycle is convenient from the town hall to the museum, and you may need to negotiate the fare.
The town center is small, so you can also explore it slowly on foot.
The exhibits are indoors, so weather matters little, but getting around Angono involves tricycles and walking, so the dry season is more comfortable.

Around November 22–23 each year, Angono holds the Higantes Festival honoring Saint Clement, and the whole town fills with giant puppets and processions. Check the Angono municipal announcements for festival dates and events.

The quietest time is usually a weekday morning. On weekends and school breaks, student groups and families increase and the halls can get crowded, so a weekday morning is recommended if you want to view the paintings slowly.

blocks.label: Season at a glance
rows: Easiest for walking, and close to festival season.
Plan around indoor viewing during the day.
Bring an umbrella and visit in the morning to avoid afternoon showers.

The museum garden has a café where you can rest with coffee and light snacks. Angono town has several restaurants serving local food, and since it is a lakeside town, many visitors look for freshwater fish dishes and Filipino home cooking. Business names change often, so it is better to look and choose on the spot. After the museum visit, many visitors sit on the garden chairs and talk about the paintings they have just seen, and workshops or events sometimes take place in the courtyard in front of the gallery. For event schedules, check the announcements on the museum's Facebook page.

Because it is an easy day trip, most people base themselves in central Manila or Antipolo. There are small hotels and guesthouses in Angono if you want to stay, but the choice is limited, so check current listings on a booking app.
Before you go, check opening hours and admission by calling (02) 8651-0048 or through the museum's Facebook page.
The exhibit follows the order of the family members, so starting at the first section and going in order makes it easier to follow.
The fisherman's festival mural has many figures, so look for them slowly with your own eyes rather than through a zoomed phone photo.
Ask the staff at the entrance whether photography is allowed.
If you want to buy a gallery work, check in advance about cash, packing and how to take it home.
In the shadeless midday hours bring a hat and water, and agree on the tricycle fare before you ride.
Combining the visit with the nearby Angono art town makes your travel more efficient.
There is a record that the museum reopened in early October 2020 after the COVID closure, so it is best to ask ahead about group visits or special event openings.
Opening hours and admission differ between sources and the museum may close on Mondays and public holidays, so be sure to check before you visit.
Manila East Road is very congested at commuting hours, so allow plenty of travel time.
Do not touch the artworks, and do not use a flash without permission.
Tricycles have no fare chart, so agree on the destination and price before riding.
Stops and terminal locations can change, so check the latest information before you leave.
Keep valuables close to your body and look after your belongings in crowded places.
The town center, about
5–10 minutes
from the museum by tricycle, gathers galleries, street murals and festival culture.

blocks.title: Tanay Old Town and San Ildefonso Church

children.text: This lakeside old town, about
1 hour
away by car, lets you see a Spanish-era church and the town together.
A city with a pilgrimage site and scenic viewpoints in Rizal, it is a good stop on the way back toward Manila.
A spot with lake and wind turbine views that you can reach by car from Angono and add to a full-day plan.
